opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the really striking thing, from a scientific point of view, is how much all children have in common. Take any two-year-old, anywhere in the world, from any background, and that child is doing something extraordinary. They're figuring out how the physical world works, how other people's minds work, how language works, and they're doing it faster and more effectively than any scientist, or for that matter any AI system we've built. That's the big puzzle: how is it possible for any human being to learn so much from so little?

When we focus on differences in intelligence, on whether this child is a little ahead of that one, we're looking at the small variations on top of that enormous common achievement. It's a bit like being fascinated by whether one person is five foot ten and another is six foot, when the really interesting question is how anyone grows at all.

I also think the focus on individual differences comes from a particular cultural picture, a kind of schooling-and-testing picture, where intelligence is a single quantity you can rank people on. But from an evolutionary perspective, the capacities that matter are the ones every human shares: the ability to explore, to imagine alternatives, to learn from other people. Those are what make us the species we are.

And there's a practical side, too. If you think of children as having more or less of some fixed thing, you start trying to optimize them, to shape them into a particular kind of adult. I've argued that's the wrong model. Parenting is less like being a carpenter and more like being a gardener. You provide a rich, safe, stable environment, and the universal capacities children have for learning and exploration will do the rest, often in ways you couldn't have predicted. The variability that matters most isn't a ranking, it's that every child takes those shared capacities in a new direction.

r001.rationale: The response frames the puzzle as how children learn so much from so little, but it does not identify how a child’s brain supports those capacities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that from the point of view of a developmental psychologist, the really striking thing about children is how much they all do. Every typically developing two-year-old has learned a language, has figured out that other people have minds, has figured out that objects persist when they're hidden, has built an intuitive physics and an intuitive psychology. And none of them were taught those things in any explicit way. So the question that I find genuinely puzzling is, how is that possible at all? How does a brain that starts out knowing relatively little end up knowing so much in just a few years? Variation in IQ is a very small signal sitting on top of that enormous common achievement.

The second thing is that the measures we use for individual differences, IQ tests and so forth, were designed for a particular purpose, which was sorting people in schools and in the army. They weren't designed to tell us anything about how the mind actually works. If you're interested in the mechanisms of learning, the way a computer scientist or a philosopher would be, then what you want to know is what the system is doing when it works, not where it falls on a bell curve.

And there's a third, more Darwinian point. Childhood is this weird, extended, costly period that human beings have more than any other species. The evolutionary explanation for that isn't that some children are a bit smarter than others. It's that the species as a whole has settled on a strategy of exploration early and exploitation later, where children's brains are built to be wide open to the world, to try lots of hypotheses, to be, as I sometimes say, lanterns rather than spotlights. That's a shared design feature, and to me, it's much more interesting than ranking the lanterns.

r001.rationale: Gopnik calls it puzzling how a brain that starts knowing relatively little ends up knowing so much in a few years, directly identifying the question that motivates her interest.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we tend to take for granted the things that all children can do, when those are often the most astonishing things. Every typically developing three-year-old can learn a language, figure out something about how other people think, and work out how to get what they want in a completely unfamiliar situation. Those are enormously difficult computational problems.

If you focus on differences in intelligence, you’re asking why one child does a little better than another on a particular task. That’s a legitimate question. But the question that fascinates me is: How does any child manage to learn so much about the world from so little evidence?

It’s also easy to confuse what we can measure with what needs explaining. We have tests that distinguish children from one another. We’re much less good at measuring the everyday learning that they all do, because it’s so pervasive that we hardly notice it. For me, that’s where the deepest scientific puzzle is.

r001.rationale: The response says the motivating puzzle is how children learn so much from little evidence, but it does not identify how a child's brain supports those capacities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you think about it, even the most ordinary four-year-old can do things that we don’t really understand how any system could do. They can figure out what other people are thinking, learn a new language, work out how the world around them operates—all from rather limited evidence. Those are extraordinary achievements, even though they’re so familiar that we tend to take them for granted.

Differences in intelligence are interesting, of course. But for me, the deeper question is: How is any of this possible? What is it about children that allows them to learn so much, so quickly? Focusing on what they share gives us a way of getting at those fundamental questions about the human mind.

r001.rationale: The response asks how children learn so much and what makes their capacities possible, but it does not identify how a child’s brain supports those capacities as the motivating question.
